newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Mortars, artillery pound junction north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Mortars, artillery pound junction north of Kabul.

text.p: Taleban forces and troops loyal to Afghanistan's ousted government battled for a second straight day to control the Bagram junction about 60 km (40 miles) north of Kabul, witnesses said on Thursday.

Reporters positioned a few kilometres (miles) north of the junction listened as shells shrieked overhead for the better part of an hour, slamming into nearby hillsides and mud-walled settlements and sending spikes of dirt and smoke into the clear blue skies as the two sides traded mortar and artillery fire.
Troops at a nearby checkpoint confirmed that the fighting was for control of the junction, which Taleban took on Wednesday.
Reports from the two sides in the battle were sharply contradictory.
In Kabul, the Taleban said earlier on Thursday it had rolled back Masood's forces from positions close to the capital Kabul and was advancing north.

Taleban-held Radio Afghanistan said its forces had retaken the village of Qarabagh, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, and a crossroads leading to Bagram airbase, the scene of heavy fighting since Masood's forces swept south late last week.

"In continuation of its mopping up operations, the Islamic army cleared Qarabagh and Chaikal-Robat up to the Bagram intersection completely of the forces of evil and corruption," Taleban-controlled Radio Afghanistan said.
In contrast, troops loyal to the former government said an attempted Taleban advance north towards Charikar to the north was beaten back very early on Thursday morning.

Witnesses said the fight could turn sharply in the deposed government's favour later in the day if, as former military chief Ahmad Shah Masood expects, reinforcements from northern Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum materialise by noon.
"They (Dostum) troops will come today...I expect them here around noon," said Masood spokesman Dr. Abdullah.

"The troops will take up positions between Charikar and the frontline (Bagram) and their heavy weapons will be back from the front line, where they should be (militarily), in accordance with the agreements made by the Afghan defense council."
Masood, a Tajik, and Dostum have been rivals and sometime enemies in the years since mujahideen forces entered Kabul and formed a government in 1992.

The threat both now perceive from the Pashtun-dominated, ultra-conservative Islamic Taleban has led them to contemplate military cooperation through a recntly-formed and broadly-based Afghan defense council.

Charikar was shuttered and virtually abandoned as civilians either fled north or sought shelter indoors from the shelling, and from warplanes which bombed the town in recent days and which could be heard overhead again on Thursday.
The Bagram junction is important because it controls traffic north and south on the main highway, also known as the "old road", connecting Kabul to northern Afghanistan through the Salang Pass.

The junction also controls access from the south to the Bagram military airfield about ten km (six miles) to the northeast. There has been fighting around the airfield for the better part of a week with no clear outcome.

Abdullah confirmed to reporters that the Taleban also hold what is known as the "new road" from Kabul to the airfield, which runs parallel to the old road and just to the east, and also the spur which links the two roads at the Bagram junction.

Commenting on peace talks underway in the Dostum stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif, Abdullah said Masood was sending a representative on Thursday after his delegate, Ahmed Mosajshid, was prevented from attending on Wednesday by poor weather which grounded his helicopter.

Masood's spokesman said there was unity among the members of the Afghan defense council that negotiation is preferable to continued fighting if the impasse over control of Afghanistan can be resolved in such a manner.
